attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post. It is not one of the tweets he quotes.

semantics.note: 'Pretty much all' is fairly rendered as 'nearly all', and 'completely ridiculous' as 'ridiculous'. It is a firm claim about current opinion in the AI community.

contract.note: Reading the claim as overwhelming consensus, not unanimity, is ordinary. Requiring representative evidence of field-wide opinion fits a claim about 'pretty much all' of a community. The early-June window is reasonable.

evidence.note: Fortune, June 13, 2022: prominent researchers on Twitter agreed Lemoine was wrong. A visible sample of prominent voices, including Marcus himself, with no sampling frame. It does not measure the whole field.
ABC, June 15, 2022, reports an expert consensus that LaMDA is not conscious. This is broad skepticism, but it does not measure prevalence or the stronger 'ridiculous' attitude.

reviews.rationale: The press reports show widespread, visible expert skepticism. Neither gives a representative measure of the community, or shows that nearly everyone found the possibility ridiculous rather than just unsupported. No counterevidence shows substantial dissent either. The packet does not settle it.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post. The Dietterich tweet is quoted separately.

semantics.note: Both parts, the wish to drop the test and the belief that beating it means nothing, are kept, and the community-versus-public scope is preserved. It is a sweeping, partly rhetorical generalization, but it is stated as fact.

contract.note: Reading 'we all' as broad consensus is fair. The support condition requires both parts. The contradiction condition sensibly asks for a substantial constituency, not isolated defenders.

evidence.note: The SEP entry, last revised Oct 2021, says opinion is divided and some still endorse the test. It predates the target period, covers mainly the philosophical literature, and gives no prevalence in the AI community in June 2022.

reviews.rationale: The only item is a pre-period scholarly overview. It shows the test still has defenders, but not how many or how active they were in the AI community in June 2022. Nothing measures the claimed wish to abandon the test. The packet does not settle either part.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence. The Roger Moore tweet that follows is a separate quotation.

semantics.note: Faithful to both parts: 'doesn't even try to connect to the world', and 'just' autocomplete predicting words in context.

contract.note: Marcus contrasts LaMDA with navigation systems that connect their bits to the world, which supports a functional reading. Treating explicit external grounding as 'trying to connect' is ordinary. The Searle-style semantic reading is flagged, and the result depends on this choice.

evidence.note: The LaMDA paper (developer authors, Feb 2022) describes fine-tuning LaMDA to consult a toolset of retrieval, calculator and translator to ground its answers. This is a developer source, which the contract specifically requires for technical design.

Google's blog post (company disclosure, Jan 2022) confirms next-token pretraining, plus safety and quality classifiers, response ranking and grounding. It shows the system is more than autocomplete alone.

reviews.rationale: The developers' own documentation from early 2022 says LaMDA was trained to call external retrieval and other tools to ground factual claims, and to filter and rank responses with classifiers. That contradicts 'doesn't even try to connect to the world' and 'just' autocomplete for the system as described. Next-token prediction is accurate only for the base model.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Correctly isolates the firm claim of 'zero lasting contribution' from the hedged 'I doubt' remark about name recognition.

contract.note: 'Zero' is absolute. Counting documented technical reuse in later AI systems, while excluding publicity, is a fair reading. A field-level reading, meaning a contribution to AI progress, would favour Marcus, and the contract flags that ambiguity.

evidence.note: A project participant's Habr account (Jan 2023) says the Emelya robot was built on Goostman's reworked language-analysis system, released May 2017 and studied in 2018. It is an insider account with no independent audit.
A 2016 peer-reviewed study used Goostman as a test subject alongside other systems. That is research use, not a lasting contribution traceable to Goostman.

reviews.rationale: Under the contract, documented later reuse of Goostman's technology shows a nonzero legacy. A dated developer-side account traces Emelya's language engine to Goostman, with release in 2017. This is narrow, rests on an insider source, and shows no foundational advance for the field. It still contradicts 'zero'.
